reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive dystrophinopathy caused by variants in the DMD gene that reduce but do not abolish functional dystrophin, producing a milder phenotype than Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Variants are typically in-frame, preserving some semi-functional dystrophin, which explains the later onset and slower progression
Presents with proximal lower-limb weakness, calf hypertrophy, cramps, and exercise intolerance, often later in childhood or adulthood
Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated even in mildly affected or minimally symptomatic individuals
Dilated cardiomyopathy can be disproportionate to skeletal muscle weakness and may dominate the clinical picture
Female carriers can develop cardiomyopathy and occasionally skeletal muscle symptoms, so they warrant cardiac surveillance
Diagnosis is confirmed by DMD molecular genetic testing, supported by muscle biopsy showing reduced or patchy dystrophin when needed
Management is multidisciplinary, with regular cardiac and respiratory monitoring, physiotherapy, and heart-failure therapy as indicated
reference.pathophysiology: Becker muscular dystrophy is caused by DMD gene variants that reduce the quantity or quality of dystrophin, a cytoskeletal protein linking the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix through the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. Because the variants are usually in-frame, some partially functional dystrophin is still produced, so membrane stabilisation is impaired rather than absent. Repeated contraction-induced sarcolemmal damage leads to calcium influx, fibre necrosis, and progressive replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue, but at a slower rate than in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The same protein deficiency in cardiac muscle causes dilated cardiomyopathy, which can be severe even when skeletal weakness is mild.
additionalDifferentials: Metabolic myopathies presenting with exercise intolerance
additionalInvestigations: DMD molecular genetic testing including deletion/duplication and sequence analysis
Muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunostaining in selected cases
Electrocardiography and echocardiography or cardiac MRI for cardiomyopathy
Pulmonary function testing to monitor respiratory involvement
Carrier testing and cardiac screening for at-risk female relatives
redFlags: Symptoms of heart failure or arrhythmia from dilated cardiomyopathy
Progressive respiratory insufficiency or nocturnal hypoventilation
Rapid loss of ambulation suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
Cardiac decompensation during anaesthesia or acute illness
New cardiac symptoms in a known female carrier
reference.prognosis: Progression is slower than in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and many patients remain ambulant well into adulthood with a substantially longer life expectancy. Cardiomyopathy is often the main determinant of prognosis, so cardiac surveillance and timely heart-failure treatment are essential.
pitfalls: Attributing raised creatine kinase to exercise or statins and missing an underlying dystrophinopathy
Focusing on skeletal weakness and overlooking a cardiomyopathy that may be more severe
Assuming female carriers are asymptomatic and neglecting their cardiac surveillance
Confusing Becker with a limb-girdle muscular dystrophy without genetic confirmation
Underusing cardiac imaging in patients with mild or subclinical muscle disease
management: Provide multidisciplinary neuromuscular care with physiotherapy to maintain mobility, prevent contractures and avoid overwork weakness
Screen for and treat dilated cardiomyopathy with heart-failure therapy such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers, since cardiac disease often determines prognosis
Undertake regular cardiac surveillance with electrocardiography and echocardiography or cardiac MRI, independent of skeletal muscle severity
Monitor respiratory function with spirometry and provide ventilatory and cough-assist support as weakness progresses
Provide orthoses, mobility aids and occupational-therapy input to preserve function, considering corticosteroids in selected patients
Offer genetic counselling for this X-linked disorder, with carrier testing and cardiac screening of at-risk female relatives
Escalate to advanced heart-failure services and consider cardiac transplantation for refractory cardiomyopathy
